Sequential Decisions: The Stagecoach Problem

Four Legs from A to J

  • A traveler crosses from town A to town J in four legs by stagecoach
  • Each leg needs a life insurance policy; the number on an arc is its cost
  • Which route costs the least in total?

Hillier and Lieberman’s prototype (Sec. 11.1): a gold-rush traveler in the 1800s, insured leg by leg, with the premium set by how dangerous the road is. The stages are the legs; each choice of town decides which towns are reachable next. That coupling is the whole topic.

The Cheapest Next Leg Misses the Optimum

Cheapest next leg: A–B–F–I–J, \({2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 13}\)

Better: A–D–F–I–J, \({3 + 1 + 3 + 4 = 11}\)

Paying 1 more on leg 1 saves 3 on leg 2.

The greedy rule looks one leg ahead. The cheap first leg to B leads to expensive second legs (4, 6, 7). Ask the class for a better route before the second click.

Enumerate, or Use the Stages

  • All routes: \({3 \times 3 \times 2 = 18}\). Three cost 11; the next best cost 13
  • With 10 stages of 10 towns each: \({10^9}\) routes to add up

The idea of dynamic programming

Solve the problem from the last stage: one leg from J. Then enlarge it one stage at a time, reusing the answer for the stages already solved. Each arc is used in one addition: 20 here, about 1,000 for 10 stages of 10 towns.

Count for the large case: 9 stage transitions of 10 x 10 arcs plus the first and last stages, about 900 to 1,000 additions, against a billion routes. The answer from J backward is also an answer for every town, so a traveler thrown off course still knows what to do.

Stages, States and the Bellman Recursion

Stages, States and Decisions

Term Stagecoach
Stage \({n}\) Leg \({n = 1, \dots, 4}\)
State \({s}\) Town at the start of leg \({n}\)
Decision \({x_n}\) Next town
Transition Next state is \({x_n}\)
Contribution Premium \({c_{s x_n}}\)
Value \({f^*_n(s)}\) Least cost from \({s}\) to J

At stage 2 in state C: three decisions, E, F or G.

The Recursion

The best cost from state \({s}\) at stage \({n}\) if the next town is \({x_n}\), and the best over all \({x_n}\):

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s, x_n) & {}= c_{s x_n} + f^*_{n+1}(x_n) \\[4pt] f^*_n(s) & {}= \min_{x_n} f_n(s, x_n) && \qquad f^*_5(J) = 0 \end{alignat*} \]

  • Solve stage 4 first, then 3, 2, 1: backward induction
  • \({f^*_1(A)}\) is the least total cost; the minimizers \({x^*_n}\) give the route

f_n(s, x_n): the cost of the immediate leg plus the best cost from where it lands. The star marks “already optimized over the remaining stages”. The boundary condition f*_5(J) = 0: at J the trip is over.

The Principle of Optimality

Bellman (1957)

An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision.

  • Given the current state, the best remaining decisions do not depend on how the process got there

The quotation is Bellman’s statement of the principle (Dynamic Programming, 1957, ch. III). The diagram is Hillier and Lieberman’s deterministic structure: the decision moves the process to a state that is fully determined by s_n and x_n.

What Makes a Problem a Dynamic Program

  1. The problem divides into stages, with a decision at each
  2. Each stage has a set of states: what the decision needs to know
  3. The decision at stage \({n}\) moves the state to one of stage \({n + 1}\)
  4. Given the state, the best remaining decisions ignore the past
  5. A recursion gives \({f^*_n}\) from \({f^*_{n+1}}\), solved from the last stage backward

Deterministic dynamic programming

The next state is fixed by the state and the decision. Part II lets chance pick it.

Backward Induction on a Staged Network

Stages 4 and 3

H 3 J
I 4 J
n = 3 f3(s, x3) = c + f4*(x3) f3*(s3) x3*
s3 H I
E 1 + 3 = 4 4 + 4 = 8 4 H
F 6 + 3 = 9 3 + 4 = 7 7 I
G 3 + 3 = 6 3 + 4 = 7 6 H

Stage 4 has one decision, J, so its table is just the premium to J. Stage 3: from E, going to H costs 1 + f*_4(H) = 1 + 3 = 4 and going to I costs 4 + 4 = 8, so f*_3(E) = 4 with x*_3 = H. Red numbers above the nodes are f*.

Stages 2 and 1

n = 2 f2(s, x2) = c + f3*(x2) f2*(s2) x2*
s2 E F G
B 7 + 4 = 11 4 + 7 = 11 6 + 6 = 12 11 E or F
C 3 + 4 = 7 2 + 7 = 9 4 + 6 = 10 7 E
D 4 + 4 = 8 1 + 7 = 8 5 + 6 = 11 8 E or F
n = 1 f1(s, x1) = c + f2*(x1) f1*(s1) x1*
s1 B C D

B ties between E and F at 11; D ties between E and F at 8; A ties between C and D at 11. Every tie is kept: each one is a second optimal decision.

Reading the Routes Forward

  • Stage 1: \({x^*_1}\) = C or D
  • From C: E, then H, then J
  • From D: E (then H, J) or F (then I, J)

Three optimal routes, cost 11

A–C–E–H–J
A–D–E–H–J
A–D–F–I–J

The tables are read forward: x*_1 from the stage 1 table, then the row of the town it leads to in the stage 2 table, and so on. B and G are off every optimal route, but their rows still say what to do if the traveler ends up there.

Dynamic Programming and the Shortest Path Algorithm

The stagecoach is a shortest path problem; lecture 06’s algorithm also finds 11.

Shortest path algorithm Dynamic programming
Order Nodes, nearest first Stages, last first
Work per step Scan the solved nodes’ neighbors One addition per arc
Networks Any, lengths \({\ge 0}\) Staged, lengths of any sign
Result Best paths from the origin A decision for every state

When the network comes in stages

Dynamic programming uses the stages: no search for the next nearest node, and the answer is a policy for every state.

Dijkstra needs nonnegative lengths; a staged network has no cycles, so dynamic programming handles negative premiums (rebates) as well. The policy view matters once chance enters in Part II: the next state is not known in advance, so a plan must say what to do in every state.

Distribution of Effort: Allocating Medical Teams

Five Medical Teams, Three Countries

Additional person-years of life, in thousands
Teams Country 1 Country 2 Country 3
0 0 0 0
1 45 20 50
2 70 45 70
3 90 75 80
4 105 110 100
5 120 150 130
  • A health council has five medical teams for three low-income countries
  • Teams stay intact: each country gets a whole number of them
  • Decide how many teams each country gets, to maximize the total person-years of life added

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 2 (the World Health Council). The measure is increased life expectancy times population. Country 2’s column grows slowly and then fast: no simple ranking of countries works.

Countries as Stages, Teams Left as the State

  • Stage \({n}\): country \({n}\); decision \({x_n}\): its teams
  • State \({s_n}\): teams still free; \({s_1 = 5}\), \({s_{n+1} = s_n - x_n}\)
  • \({p_n(x_n)}\): person-years from the table

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s_n, x_n) & {}= p_n(x_n) + f^*_{n+1}(s_n - x_n) \\[4pt] f^*_n(s_n) & {}= \max_{x_n = 0, \dots, s_n} f_n(s_n, x_n) \end{alignat*} \]

Country 3 takes every team left: \({f^*_3(s_3) = p_3(s_3)}\).

An arc from \({s_2}\) to \({s_3}\) earns \({p_2(s_2 - s_3)}\): the best path is the best allocation.

What Dynamic Programming Assumes

Linear programming (LP) assumption LP This problem
Proportionality Needed Not needed: \({p_n}\) is any table
Divisibility Needed Not needed: teams are whole
Additivity Needed Needed: the total is \({p_1 + p_2 + p_3}\)
Certainty Needed Needed here; Part II drops it

Distribution of effort

One resource shared among activities, each with its own return table. Dynamic programming needs only that the returns add up.

Hillier and Lieberman’s point in Sec. 11.3: of the four LP assumptions, the distribution of effort problem needs only additivity. Other examples: salespeople to regions, scientists to research teams, ad budget to media.

Knapsack Problems: Capacity as the State

Loading a Truck

Load A B C D
Pallets 2 3 4 5
Pays ($100s) 7 11 10 12
Per pallet 3.5 3.67 2.5 2.4
  • The truck holds 7 pallets; each load goes whole or not at all
  • Best pay per pallet first: B, then A: \({11 + 7 = 18}\), 2 pallets empty

As an integer program (IP), \({x_i = 1}\) if load \({i}\) goes:

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \max~ & \rlap{7x_A + 11x_B + 10x_C + 12x_D} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & 2x_A + 3x_B + 4x_C + 5x_D & \quad & {}\le 7 \\ & x_A, x_B, x_C, x_D & \quad & {}\in \{0, 1\} \end{alignat*} \]

A knapsack problem: one constraint, yes-or-no items. Capital budgeting with one budget is the same model.

A carrier is offered four loads for one trip. The LP relaxation gives 23 (A, B and half of C), an upper bound; the IP optimum is 21. The greedy answer 18 leaves 2 pallets of room unused.

The Knapsack as a Dynamic Program

  • Stage \({n}\): load \({n}\) (A, B, C, D); decision \({x_n \in \{0, 1\}}\)
  • State \({s_n}\): pallets still free; \({s_1 = 7}\), \({s_{n+1} = s_n - w_n x_n}\)
  • \({x_n = 1}\) only if \({w_n \le s_n}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s_n, x_n) & {}= v_n\, x_n + f^*_{n+1}(s_n - w_n\, x_n) \\[4pt] f^*_n(s_n) & {}= \max_{x_n} f_n(s_n, x_n) && \qquad f^*_5(s) = 0 \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({w_n}\): pallets; \({v_n}\): pay. States run from 0 to 7 at every stage but the first

Loads B and C: $2,100

All 7 pallets used. gurobipy on the IP: 21, the same loads.

Three Budgets Make the State a Vector

Lecture 02’s bookstore chose among 5 projects with three yearly budgets: 150, 110 and 60 ($1,000s).

  • The state is the money left in each year: \({(b_1, b_2, b_3)}\)
  • In $1,000 steps: \({151 \times 111 \times 61 = 1{,}022{,}421}\) states per stage, against 8 for the truck

State spaces grow exponentially

The number of states grows exponentially with the number of state variables, which Bellman called “the curse of dimensionality”. By hand, the state must take a handful of values; the bookstore is a job for the IP solver.

Bellman’s phrase is in the preface of Dynamic Programming (1957). The IP solves the bookstore instantly (lecture 02, $330,000). Dynamic programming pays off when the state is small and the stage returns are nonlinear or tabulated, as in the medical teams problem.

Part II: Continuous States and Probabilistic Recursions

When the state is a number on a line, and when chance picks the next state

Discrete and Continuous States: The Endpoint Argument

Three New Products, One Plant

Product 1 2 3
Start-up cost \({c_n}\) 3 2 0
Marginal net revenue \({r_n}\) 2 3 1
Capacity per unit 20% 40% 20%
  • Starting a product costs \({c_n}\) once; each unit then adds \({r_n}\)
  • Product 1 sells at most 3 units; products 2 and 3 sell all they make
  • Decide how many units of each to make, to maximize net revenue minus start-up costs

(a) Integer units. (b) Divisible units. A past Exam 2 problem, 60 of 100 points.

Problem 2 of a past Exam 2; its solution file calls it Problem 11-2 and works it in Hillier and Lieberman’s notation. The capacity percentages are multiples of 20, which is what makes the integer state small: five blocks of 20%.

Integer Production: The State in 20% Blocks

  • Stage \({n}\): product \({n}\); decision \({x_n}\): units made
  • State \({s_n}\): 20% blocks of capacity left: \({s_1 = 5}\), \({s_2 = 5 - x_1}\), \({s_3 = s_2 - 2x_2}\)
  • Profit of \({x_n}\) units: \({p_n(x_n) = r_n x_n - c_n}\) if \({x_n > 0}\), and 0 if \({x_n = 0}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s_n, x_n) & {}= p_n(x_n) + f^*_{n+1}(s_n - w_n\, x_n) \\[4pt] f^*_n(s_n) & {}= \max_{x_n} f_n(s_n, x_n) && \qquad f^*_3(s_3) = s_3 \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({w_n}\): blocks per unit, 1, 2, 1. Product 3 has no start-up cost, so it takes every block left

Integer Production: Backward Tables

n = 3 s3 f3*(s3) x3*
0 0 0
1 1 1
2 2 2

4 4 4
5 5 5
n = 2 p2(x2) + f3*(s2 − 2x2) f2*(s2) x2*
s2 0 1 2
0 0 + 0 = 0 0 0
1 0 + 1 = 1 1 0
2 0 + 2 = 2 1 + 0 = 1 2 0
3 0 + 3 = 3 1 + 1 = 2 3 0
4 0 + 4 = 4 1 + 2 = 3 4 + 0 = 4 4 0 or 2
5 0 + 5 = 5 1 + 3 = 4 4 + 1 = 5 5 0 or 2
n = 1 p1(x1) + f2*(5 − x1) f1*(s1) x1*
s1 0 1 2 3
5 0 + 5 = 5 −1 + 4 = 3 1 + 3 = 4 3 + 2 = 5 5 0 or 3

Stage 2, s_2 = 4: x_2 = 0 gives 0 + 4; x_2 = 1 gives (3 - 2) + f*_3(2) = 1 + 2 = 3; x_2 = 2 gives (6 - 2) + 0 = 4. Ties are kept. The start-up cost is why x_2 = 1 never wins: one unit of product 2 earns 3 - 2 = 1, the same as the two blocks it uses would earn as product 3.

Three Optimal Plans

  • \({x^*_1 = 0}\): \({s_2 = 5}\), \({x^*_2 = 0}\) or 2
    • \({x_2 = 0}\): \({s_3 = 5}\), \({x_3 = 5}\)
    • \({x_2 = 2}\): \({s_3 = 1}\), \({x_3 = 1}\)
  • \({x^*_1 = 3}\): \({s_2 = 2}\), \({x^*_2 = 0}\); \({s_3 = 2}\), \({x_3 = 2}\)
Three optimal plans, profit 5
\({(x_1, x_2, x_3)}\) Profit
(0, 0, 5) \({5}\)
(0, 2, 1) \({(6 - 2) + 1 = 5}\)
(3, 0, 2) \({(6 - 3) + 2 = 5}\)

Read every tie forward

A tie in \({x^*_n}\) branches the forward pass. The exam asks for all optimal plans.

Divisible Units: Only the Endpoints Matter

  • \({s_n}\): percent of capacity left; \({s_1 = 100}\)
  • Product 3: \({f^*_3(s_3) = s_3/20}\)
  • Product 2: \({3x_2 - 2 + (s_2 - 40x_2)/20}\), linear in \({x_2 > 0}\)
  • Compare the endpoints: \({x_2 = 0}\) gives \({s_2/20}\), and \({x_2 = s_2/40}\) gives \({3s_2/40 - 2}\)
  • Equal at \({s_2 = 80}\): product 2 only if \({s_2 \ge 80}\)

The exam solution’s argument: the profit is linear in x_n except for the start-up term, so the maximum over 0 <= x_2 <= s_2/40 is at an end of the interval. The red band is f*_2(s_2): s_2/20 up to 80 and 3 s_2/40 - 2 above.

Divisible Units: Stage 1 and the Plan

\(f_1(100, x_1) = 2x_1 - 3 + f^*_2(100 - 20x_1)\) for \({0 < x_1 \le 3}\), and \({f^*_2(100)}\) for \({x_1 = 0}\).

  • \({x_1 = 0}\): \({f^*_2(100) = 3(100)/40 - 2 =}\) 5.5
  • \({x_1 = 3}\): \({6 - 3 + f^*_2(40) = 3 + 2 = 5}\)
  • \({f_1}\) rises on \({0 < x_1 \le 3}\), so these two are the candidates

Divisible optimum: 5.5

\({x_1 = 0}\), so \({s_2 = 100 \ge 80}\) and \({x_2 = 100/40 = 2.5}\); then \({s_3 = 0}\), \({x_3 = 0}\). Make 2.5 units of product 2 only. Divisibility adds 0.5 to the integer optimum.

On 0 < x_1 <= 1, s_2 is in [80, 100) and f_1 = 2.5 + 0.5 x_1; on 1 <= x_1 <= 3, s_2 is in [40, 80] and f_1 = 2 + x_1. Both pieces rise, so x_1 = 3 is the best positive level and it loses to x_1 = 0. gurobipy, with a binary for each start-up: 5.5 at (0, 2.5, 0).

Continuous States by Calculus: Employment Levels

The Local Job Shop

  • Workers needed each season: the chart, from this spring to the next
  • No overtime and no inventory: custom orders
  • A worker above the requirement costs $2,000 a season
  • Changing the level costs $200 × (change)²
  • Part-time workers make fractional levels possible

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 4. Hiring and training is costly, so management dislikes swings; idle workers are costly too. The question is how far to cut the workforce in the slack seasons.

Seasons as Stages, Last Season’s Level as the State

  • Stage \({n}\): season, \({n = 1}\) summer to \({n = 4}\) spring; decision \({x_n}\): workers employed; \({x_n \ge r_n}\) and \({x_4 = 255}\)
  • State \({s_n = x_{n-1}}\), last season’s level; \({s_1 = 255}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f^*_n(s_n) & {}= \min_{r_n \le x_n \le 255} \big\{ 200(x_n - s_n)^2 + 2000(x_n - r_n) + f^*_{n+1}(x_n) \big\} \\[4pt] f^*_4(s_4) & {}= 200(255 - s_4)^2 \end{alignat*} \]

A continuous state

\({s_n}\) can be any number in an interval: no table can list it. Each \({f^*_n}\) is a formula in \({s_n}\), minimized by setting a derivative to 0.

Winter by Calculus

\(f_3(s_3, x_3) = 200(x_3 - s_3)^2 + 2000(x_3 - 200) + 200(255 - x_3)^2\)

\[ \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_3} = 400(x_3 - s_3) + 2000 - 400(255 - x_3) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^*_3 = \frac{s_3 + 250}{2} \]

  • Autumn’s level is between 240 and 255, so \({x^*_3}\) is between 245 and 252.5: above winter’s 200
  • Substituting: \({f^*_3(s_3) = 50(250 - s_3)^2 + 50(260 - s_3)^2 + 1000(s_3 - 150)}\)

The second derivative is 800 > 0, so the stationary point is the minimum. Substitution: x*_3 - s_3 = (250 - s_3)/2 and 255 - x*_3 = (260 - s_3)/2, and 200/4 = 50.

Autumn: The Requirement Binds

\(f_2(s_2, x_2) = 200(x_2 - s_2)^2 + 2000(x_2 - 240) + f^*_3(x_2)\)

\[ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_2} = 400(x_2 - s_2) + 2000 - 100(250 - x_2) - 100(260 - x_2) + 1000 = 0 \]

Solving: \({600x_2 = 400s_2 + 48{,}000}\), so \({x_2 = (2s_2 + 240)/3}\).

  • This is \({\ge 240}\) only if \({s_2 \ge 240}\). Below, \({f_2}\) rises on \({[240, 255]}\), so \({x^*_2 = 240}\)

\[ x^*_2(s_2) = \begin{cases} 240 & 220 \le s_2 \le 240 \\[2pt] (2s_2 + 240)/3 & 240 \le s_2 \le 255 \end{cases} \]

Summer and the Plan

  • Summer: \({\partial f_1/\partial x_1 = 0}\) gives \({x^*_1 = 247.5}\) (appendix). Forward: \({x_2 = 245}\), \({x_3 = 247.5}\), \({x_4 = 255}\)
Total cost $185,000. gurobipy, as a quadratic program: the same plan
Season Level Change Surplus
Summer 247.5 11,250 55,000
Autumn 245 1,250 10,000
Winter 247.5 1,250 95,000
Spring 255 11,250 0

Change cost: 200 x 7.5^2 = 11,250 in summer (255 to 247.5), 200 x 2.5^2 = 1,250 in autumn and winter, 200 x 7.5^2 in spring. Surplus: 2,000 x 27.5, 2,000 x 5, 2,000 x 47.5, 0. The winter surplus is the largest cost and still cheaper than the swings it avoids. The notebook solves this quadratic program.

Probabilistic Recursions: Maximizing a Probability

When Chance Picks the Next State

\[ f_n(s_n, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \big[ C_i + f^*_{n+1}(i) \big], \qquad f^*_n(s_n) = \min_{x_n} f_n(s_n, x_n) \]

\({p_i}\): probability of state \({i}\) given \({s_n}\) and \({x_n}\); \({C_i}\): the contribution on that branch. Minimize an expected sum, or maximize one.

Hillier and Lieberman’s Fig. 11.10. The decision fixes the probabilities, and chance picks the next state. The recursion takes the expected value over the branches; the principle of optimality still holds, because the best decisions from state i do not depend on how the process got there.

Three Chips, Three Plays

  • A player’s system wins each play with probability \({2/3}\); a bet of \({x}\) chips wins \({x}\) or loses \({x}\)
  • The player starts with 3 chips and wins a side bet with 5 or more after 3 plays. Maximize the probability of winning it
  • Stage \({n}\): play \({n}\); state \({s_n}\): chips in hand; decision \({x_n \le s_n}\): chips bet

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s_n, x_n) & {}= \tfrac{1}{3}\, f^*_{n+1}(s_n - x_n) + \tfrac{2}{3}\, f^*_{n+1}(s_n + x_n) \\[4pt] f^*_4(s) & {}= 1 \text{ if } s \ge 5, \text{ and 0 otherwise} \end{alignat*} \]

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 6, Winning in Las Vegas. The objective is a probability, so each branch’s contribution is 0 and f* at the end is 1 or 0. Ask first: should the player bet everything on play 1?

≥ 5 1 0 to s3 − 5

s2 0 1 2 3 4

Play 3: with 3 chips, a bet of 2 or 3 reaches 5 on a win: 2/3. With 2 or fewer, 5 is out of reach. Play 2, 4 chips: a bet of 1 gives 1/3 f*_3(3) + 2/3 f*_3(5) = 1/3 x 2/3 + 2/3 x 1 = 8/9. Ties are kept.

s1 0 1 2 3

Play Chips Bet

Probability 20/27 ≈ 0.74

Bet 1 chip, then adapt: the bet at play 2 depends on what play 1 did. Betting everything at once wins only 2/3.

“Enough to reach 5”: with 3 chips bet 2 or 3; with 4 chips bet 1 to 4. With 2 chips or fewer at play 3 the side bet is lost. Check by the tree: 2/3 [2/3 + 1/3 x 2/3] + 1/3 x 4/9 = 16/27 + 4/27 = 20/27.

Expected-Cost Recursions: A State-Dependent Policy

Two Engines, Three Auctions

  • A repair shop needs two refurbished engines within three weeks
  • One engine is auctioned each week: skip, bid low or bid high. The shop pays only if it wins
  • After week 3, each missing engine costs 14 new from the dealer
  • Minimize the expected total cost
Bid Price ($1,000s) Wins
Low 3 \({1/2}\)
High 6 \({3/4}\)

Written for this course. Bidding high costs more but wins more often; skipping saves the bid and spends a week. The dealer’s price is the penalty for running out of time.

The Recursion

  • Stage \({n}\): week \({n}\); state \({s_n}\): engines still needed (0, 1, 2); decision \({x_n}\): skip, low or high
  • A bid \({b}\) that wins with probability \({p}\):

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} f_n(s, b) & {}= p\,\big[\, b + f^*_{n+1}(s - 1) \,\big] + (1 - p)\, f^*_{n+1}(s) \\[4pt] f_n(s, \text{skip}) & {}= f^*_{n+1}(s) && \qquad f^*_4(s) = 14s \end{alignat*} \]

  • Each branch has its own contribution: the bid if won, 0 if lost
  • \({f^*_n}\) is an expected cost: the recursion takes a minimum of averages

Weeks 3 and 2

n = 3 p(b + f*(s − 1)) + (1 − p) f*(s); skip: f*(s) f3*(s3) x3*
s3 Skip Low High
0 0 0 none
1 14 ½(3 + 0) + ½(14) = 8.5 ¾(6 + 0) + ¼(14) = 8 8 High
2 28 ½(3 + 14) + ½(28) = 22.5 ¾(6 + 14) + ¼(28) = 22 22 High
n = 2 p(b + f*(s − 1)) + (1 − p) f*(s); skip: f*(s) f2*(s2) x2*
s2 Skip Low High
0 0 0 none
1 8 ½(3 + 0) + ½(8) = 5.5 ¾(6 + 0) + ¼(8) = 6.5 5.5 Low
2 22 ½(3 + 8) + ½(22) = 16.5 ¾(6 + 8) + ¼(22) = 16 16 High

Week 3, one engine needed: low costs 1/2(3 + 0) + 1/2(14) = 8.5, high 3/4(6 + 0) + 1/4(14) = 8. With the dealer at 14, the higher chance is worth the higher price. Week 2, one engine: low wins 5.5 against 6.5, because a loss still leaves week 3.

Week 1 and the Policy

n = 1 p(b + f*(s − 1)) + (1 − p) f*(s); skip: f*(s) f1*(s1) x1*
s1 Skip Low High
2 16 ½(3 + 5.5) + ½(16) = 12.25 ¾(6 + 5.5) + ¼(16) = 12.625 12.25 Low
The optimal policy
Week One needed Two needed
1 Low
2 Low High
3 High High

Expected cost $12,250

Bid low while time remains; bid high when the deadline is near and engines are missing. Buying both from the dealer costs $28,000.

The policy is a rule by week and state: the decision in week 2 depends on what happened in week 1. No fixed plan of three bids, chosen in advance, can match it. Week 1, two needed: low 12.25, high 12.625, skip 16.

Part III: Markov Decision Processes and Reinforcement Learning

When there is no last stage, and when the probabilities must be learned

Markov Decision Processes and the Bellman Equation

A Shop with No Last Week

  • A shop sells a premium espresso machine. Each Monday it sees its stock \({s}\) (the room holds 3) and orders \({a}\) units; they arrive at once
  • Weekly demand is 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities \({1/4}\), \({1/2}\), \({1/4}\); a sale missed is lost
Sale price Unit cost Per order Per unit left on Sunday
$800 $400 $200 $100
  • No week is the last: a dollar next week is worth \({\gamma = 0.8}\) today. Equivalently, each week the product stays on sale with probability 0.8
  • Decide how much to order in each state, for every week

Written for this course. In $100s: price 8, cost 4, fee 2, holding 1. The discount factor can be read as interest or as the chance the product line survives another week; both give the same model.

Markov Decision Process

Markov decision process (MDP)

States \({s}\); actions \({a \in A(s)}\); transition probabilities \({p(s' \mid s, a)}\); expected reward \({r(s, a)}\); discount factor \({0 \le \gamma < 1}\). The next state depends only on the current state and action.

  • A stationary policy \({\pi}\) names an action for each state, the same every week
  • Its value: \({V^\pi(s) = E\big[\sum_{t \ge 0} \gamma^t\, r(s_t, \pi(s_t)) \mid s_0 = s\big]}\)
The shop as an MDP
State \({s}\) Action \({a}\) Reward \({r(s, a)}\)
Stock on Monday, 0 to 3 Units ordered, \({a \le 3 - s}\) Sales minus holding and order cost

The Shop’s Data

Everything after the order depends only on the stock \({y = s + a}\):

Stock y Expected sales Expected left R(y) = 8 sales − left Next stock 0 Next stock 1 Next stock 2 Next stock 3
0 0 0 0 1
1 0.75 0.25 5.75 ¾ ¼
2 1 1 7 ¼ ½ ¼
3 1 2 6 ¼ ½ ¼
  • Next stock: probabilities from the demand. Reward: \({r(s, a) = R(s + a) - (2 + 4a)}\) if \({a > 0}\), and \({R(s)}\) if \({a = 0}\)

Example, y = 2: sales are 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, mean 1; units left 2, 1, 0, mean 1. So R(2) = 8 - 1 = 7. A third unit never sells in the week it arrives (demand is at most 2), so R(3) = 6 < 7; it is worth stocking only for next week.

The Bellman Equation

\[ V^*(s) = \max_{a \in A(s)} \Big\{ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\, V^*(s') \Big\} \qquad \text{for every } s \]

  • Part II’s recursion with the stage index dropped: every week looks the same, so \({f^*_n}\) becomes one function \({V^*}\)
  • Four equations in four unknowns, with a max: no direct solve

Two ways to solve it

Value iteration: apply the right-hand side again and again. Linear programming: the smallest \({V}\) that satisfies every “\({\ge}\)” version of the equation.

Bellman (1957) wrote the stationary equation as well as the finite-stage recursion. gamma < 1 keeps the sum of discounted rewards finite.

Value Iteration and Linear Programming

Value Iteration

  1. Start from \({V_0(s) = 0}\) for every \({s}\)
  2. Sweep: \({V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \big\{ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\, V_k(s') \big\}}\)
  3. Stop when \({\max_s |V_{k+1}(s) - V_k(s)|}\) is small; act greedily on \({V_{k+1}}\)
  • \({V_k}\) is the best expected profit over \({k}\) weeks: \({k}\) stages of Part II
  • Each sweep cuts the error at least by the factor \({\gamma}\): after \({k}\) sweeps it is at most \({\gamma^k}\) times the first error

One sweep for the shop, in two steps

\({G_k(y) = R(y) + 0.8 \sum p(\text{next} \mid y)\, V_k(\text{next})}\), then \({V_{k+1}(s) = \max_{y \ge s} \{ G_k(y) - \text{order cost} \}}\), with order cost \({2 + 4(y - s)}\) if \({y > s}\)

Sweep 1 by Hand

\({V_0 = 0}\), so \({G_0(y) = R(y)}\): 0, 5.75, 7, 6.

sweep 1 G0(y) − order cost, by stock after ordering y V1(s) order
s 0 1 2 3
0 0 5.75 − 6 = −0.25 7 − 10 = −3 6 − 14 = −8 0 0
1 5.75 7 − 6 = 1 6 − 10 = −4 5.75 0
2 7 6 − 6 = 0 7 0
3 6 6 0

With one week left, ordering never pays

A unit bought for $400 plus the $200 fee cannot earn it back in one week: \({5.75 - 6 < 0}\) from an empty shelf.

Row s = 0: no order gives 0; ordering 1 gives R(1) - (2 + 4) = -0.25; ordering 2 gives 7 - 10 = -3; ordering 3 gives 6 - 14 = -8. V_1 is the best expected profit if the world ended after this week.

Sweep 2 by Hand

y R(y) 0.8 × expected V(next) G(y)
0 0 0.8(0) = 0 0
1 5.75 0.2(5.75) + 0.6(0) = 1.15 6.9
2 7 0.2(7) + 0.4(5.75) + 0.2(0) = 3.7 10.7
3 6 0.2(6) + 0.4(7) + 0.2(5.75) = 5.15 11.15
sweep 2 G1(y) − order cost, by stock after ordering y V2(s) order
s 0 1 2 3
0 0 6.9 − 6 = 0.9 10.7 − 10 = 0.7 11.15 − 14 = −2.85 0.9 1
1 6.9 10.7 − 6 = 4.7 11.15 − 10 = 1.15 6.9 0
2 10.7 11.15 − 6 = 5.15 10.7 0
3 11.15 11.15 0

Weights: 0.8 x 1/4 = 0.2 and 0.8 x 1/2 = 0.4. y = 2: 7 + 0.2 V_1(2) + 0.4 V_1(1) + 0.2 V_1(0) = 7 + 1.4 + 2.3 + 0 = 10.7. With two weeks counted, an empty shop orders 1: 6.9 - 6 = 0.9 > 0. From sweep 3 on it orders 2.

The Optimal Policy

Exact values by solving the Bellman equation for this policy
Stock \({s}\) \({V^*(s)}\) ($100s) Order
0 6.25 2

Order 2 when the shelf is empty

A reorder point of 0 and an order-up-to level of 2: an \({(s, S)}\) policy. The fee makes small, frequent orders expensive.

  • The policy settled at sweep 3; the values took 31 sweeps to come within 0.01 of \({V^*}\)

V(2) - V(0) = 10 exactly: from 0, ordering 2 costs 2 + 8 = 10 and leaves the shop in the same position as starting with 2. Exact values: 25/4, 95/8, 65/4, 595/32.

The Bellman Equation as an LP

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{\textstyle\sum_s V(s)} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & V(s) - \gamma \textstyle\sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\, V(s') & \quad & {}\ge r(s, a) && \qquad \text{every } s, a \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({V(s)}\) free in sign. One variable per state, one constraint per state and action: 4 and 10 for the shop
  • gurobipy: \({V = (6.25, 11.875, 16.25, 18.59)}\); the tight constraints are the optimal actions

Lecture 04 again

The dual’s variables are discounted state-action frequencies: how often the policy takes action \({a}\) in state \({s}\). Weak and strong duality hold as for any LP.

Any V that satisfies all “>=” constraints is an upper bound on V, so the smallest one is V. The four tight rows are (s=0, order 2) and (s, order 0) for s = 1, 2, 3. The notebook builds this LP.

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def f(n, s):
    if n == len(loads):
        return 0
    name, w, v = loads[n]
    return max(f(n + 1, s), v + f(n + 1, s - w)) if w <= s else f(n + 1, s)

Reinforcement Learning: Q-Learning from Samples

When the Probabilities Are Unknown

  • Value iteration needs \({p(s' \mid s, a)}\). A new product has no demand history
  • The Q-factor of a state and action: \({Q^*(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\, V^*(s')}\)
  • Then \({V^*(s) = \max_a Q^*(s, a)}\), and the best action is the \({a}\) that attains it

Learn Q from experience

Each week shows one sample: state \({s}\), action \({a}\), reward \({r}\), next state \({s'}\). Reinforcement learning estimates \({Q^*}\) from such samples, without writing \({p}\) down.

Q-Learning

After each observed step \({(s, a, r, s')}\):

\[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \,\Big] \]

  • The bracket is the error in the Bellman equation, measured on one sample
  • \({\alpha}\): the step size, or learning rate
  • Explore: now and then try an action other than the best so far

Watkins and Dayan (1992)

Q-learning converges to \({Q^*}\) if every state-action pair is tried infinitely often and the step sizes shrink suitably.

Same equation as value iteration; the expectation over s’ is replaced by the one s’ the world produced, and alpha averages the samples over time. No code here: the idea is what matters for the exam.

Powell’s Unified Framework

Every sequential decision problem has five parts (Powell, 2019, 2022):

Part The shop
State \({S_t}\) Stock on Monday
Decision \({x_t}\) Units ordered
New information \({W_{t+1}}\) The week’s demand
Transition \({S_{t+1} = S^M(S_t, x_t, W_{t+1})}\) Stock left on Sunday
Objective Expected discounted profit, over policies
  • Four classes of policies: rules (order up to 2), modified deterministic models, value function approximations (this lecture), and lookahead models (lecture 05’s stochastic programs)

Sutton and Barto: Reinforcement Learning

  • An agent acts in an environment, receives rewards and learns a policy by trial and error; the MDP is the model behind it
  • Three families: value-based (Q-learning), policy-based (adjust the policy along the gradient of its value), model-based (learn \({p}\), then plan)
  • When the states are too many to list, a function approximates \({V}\) or \({Q}\); with a neural network, this is deep reinforcement learning

The bridge

The Bellman equation of this lecture is the equation those methods solve, from samples, when the transition probabilities are unknown.

Sutton and Barto (2018) is the standard text. Powell’s framework and Sutton and Barto’s book describe the same problem class from operations research and from computer science.

Where Sequential Decisions Appear

Schneider National’s fleet planning used approximate dynamic programming (Simão et al., 2009); backgammon (Tesauro, 1995) and Go (Silver et al., 2016) by reinforcement learning
Application State Decision
Inventory Stock on hand Units to order
Revenue management Seats left, days to departure Fares to offer
Maintenance Condition of a machine Repair, replace or wait
Truckload fleets Drivers and loads by city Which driver takes which load
Games Board position Next move

Conclusions

Summary of Part I

Core takeaways

  • Stages, states, decisions; the recursion \({f^*_n(s) = \min_x \{c + f^*_{n+1}\}}\)
  • Solve backward, read forward
  • The state is what the next decision needs to know

Watch out for

  • Ties: keep every \({x^*_n}\), they branch the forward pass
  • Infeasible decisions: leave the cell blank
  • A vector state: the states multiply

Summary of Part II

Core takeaways

  • Continuous state: \({f^*_n}\) is a formula; endpoints or calculus
  • Probabilistic: \({f_n = \sum_i p_i [C_i + f^*_{n+1}(i)]}\)
  • The answer is a policy: a decision for each state

Watch out for

  • Start-up costs break linearity at 0
  • Check that a stationary point is feasible
  • Each branch has its own contribution

Summary of Part III

Core takeaways

  • No last stage: discount, drop \({n}\), the Bellman equation
  • Value iteration converges; the policy often settles first
  • The MDP is also an LP

Watch out for

  • \({\gamma < 1}\) is what keeps values finite
  • Q-learning trades the model for samples and exploration

Bottom line

Name the stages and the state first; the recursion follows from them.

Appendix: Summer by Calculus

For \({s_2 \ge 240}\), the slope of \({f^*_2}\) is that of its first term at \({x^*_2}\):

\[ \frac{d f^*_2}{d s_2} = -400\,(x^*_2 - s_2) = -400 \Big( \frac{2s_2 + 240}{3} - s_2 \Big) = \frac{400}{3}(s_2 - 240) \]

With \({s_2 = x_1}\):

\[ \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} = 400(x_1 - 255) + 2000 + \frac{400}{3}(x_1 - 240) = 0 \]

Times 3: \({1200x_1 - 306{,}000 + 6{,}000 + 400x_1 - 96{,}000 = 0}\), so \({1600x_1 = 396{,}000}\) and \({x^*_1 = 247.5}\).

  • On \({220 \le x_1 \le 240}\) the slope is \({800x_1 - 196{,}000 < 0}\): no minimum there
